subject: geography
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: In the Demographic Transition Model, Stage 1 is characterised by:
options: Low birth rates and low death rates
Falling birth rates and rising death rates
High birth rates and low death rates
High birth rates and high death rates, giving low natural increase
questions.explain: Stage 1 has high fluctuating birth and death rates, producing a stable, low total population.

questions.q: The 'demographic dividend' refers to the potential economic boost when:
options: Net migration falls to zero
Birth rates suddenly rise
The dependent elderly population dominates
A large share of the population is of working age relative to dependants
questions.explain: A demographic dividend occurs when a country has a large working-age population relative to dependants, boosting growth potential.

questions.q: Ester Boserup's counter-argument to Malthus was that:
options: Food supply can never be increased
Necessity is the mother of invention, so population pressure drives agricultural innovation
Population growth is always disastrous
War is the only check on population
questions.explain: Boserup argued that population pressure stimulates innovation and intensification, increasing food production to meet demand.

questions.q: A youthful population structure typically shows a population pyramid with:
options: A narrow base and wide top
A wide base reflecting high birth rates and a large proportion of children
No people under 15
Equal width at all ages
questions.explain: A youthful population has a wide pyramid base, indicating high birth rates and a large share of young dependants.

questions.q: An ageing population is most directly caused by:
options: Falling birth rates combined with rising life expectancy
A sudden epidemic of childhood disease
Rising birth rates and falling life expectancy
High youthful in-migration only
questions.explain: Ageing populations result from declining fertility and increasing longevity, raising the proportion of elderly people.

questions.q: Thomas Malthus argued that:
options: Food supply would always exceed population needs
Population could never increase
Innovation would always solve resource shortages
Population would grow geometrically and outstrip food supply, which grows arithmetically
questions.explain: Malthus argued population grows geometrically while food supply grows only arithmetically, so population would outstrip food.

questions.q: In Lee's model, 'intervening obstacles' refer to:
options: Government subsidies for migration
The age of the migrant
Barriers such as cost, distance or border controls that lie between origin and destination
Pull factors at the destination
questions.explain: Intervening obstacles are barriers between origin and destination, such as physical distance, cost and immigration controls.

questions.q: A potential social impact of large-scale immigration on a host area is:
options: Greater cultural diversity but possible community tensions
An immediate fall in the host population
Automatic elimination of all unemployment
The disappearance of all public services
questions.explain: Immigration can enrich host societies with diversity but may also generate social tensions over integration and resources.

questions.q: Environmental conditions can influence population distribution because:
options: Climate has no effect on settlement
Soil fertility is irrelevant to population
People prefer the most extreme deserts
Climate and water availability strongly shape where people can settle densely
questions.explain: Physical factors such as climate, relief, water and soil fertility strongly influence where populations cluster or remain sparse.

questions.q: In Lee's migration model, 'push factors' are best described as:
options: The personal characteristics of the migrant
Barriers preventing movement
Attractive features drawing people to a destination
Negative conditions in the origin that encourage people to leave
questions.explain: Push factors are negative aspects of the origin area, such as unemployment or conflict, that prompt people to leave.

questions.q: An 'optimum population' is one where:
options: Population is at its absolute maximum
The number of people best matches resources to maximise output per head
Population is zero
Death rates exceed birth rates
questions.explain: Optimum population is the level at which resources are used most efficiently to give the highest standard of living per person.

questions.q: The carrying capacity of an environment is best defined as:
options: The average rainfall
The maximum population it can support sustainably with available resources
The total land area in square kilometres
The number of migrants entering per year
questions.explain: Carrying capacity is the largest population an environment can support sustainably given its resources.

questions.q: A 'Malthusian check' is best described as:
options: A government subsidy for large families
An increase in food production
A technological breakthrough in farming
A factor such as famine, disease or war that limits population growth
questions.explain: Malthusian positive checks such as famine, disease and war raise the death rate to bring population back in line with resources.

questions.q: The proposed Stage 5 of the Demographic Transition Model is marked by:
options: Birth rates falling below death rates, causing natural decline
Death rates falling to zero
A return to high birth rates
No change from Stage 4
questions.explain: In Stage 5 birth rates drop below death rates, leading to natural population decline and an ageing structure.

questions.q: China's former One-Child Policy is an example of:
options: An epidemiological transition
A migration corridor
An anti-natalist policy aimed at reducing the birth rate
A pro-natalist policy
questions.explain: The One-Child Policy was an anti-natalist measure designed to slow rapid population growth by limiting family size.

questions.q: Stage 4 of the Demographic Transition Model is characterised by:
options: Low birth rates and low death rates, giving a stable high population
Rapidly rising death rates
High birth and high death rates
A birth rate of zero
questions.explain: Stage 4 has low and stable birth and death rates, resulting in a high but largely stable total population.

questions.q: Forced migration is best illustrated by:
options: A student relocating for university
People fleeing a civil war as refugees
A graduate moving abroad for a higher salary
A retiree moving to the coast
questions.explain: Forced migration involves people compelled to move by conflict, persecution or disaster, such as war refugees.

questions.q: A common economic impact of out-migration on a source area is:
options: A total collapse in remittance income
Loss of working-age, economically active people, often called a brain drain
A surge in the local labour supply
An immediate rise in the birth rate
questions.explain: Out-migration often removes young, skilled, working-age people, producing a brain drain in the source area.

questions.q: Which of the following is a classic 'pull factor' for migration?
options: Better job opportunities and higher wages at the destination
High unemployment in the origin
Drought in the home area
Political persecution at home
questions.explain: Pull factors are positive attractions of a destination, such as employment, higher wages and better services.

questions.q: Step migration describes a process in which migrants:
options: Never relocate
Move only across international borders
Move through a series of stages, for example village to town to city
Move directly to a megacity in one move
questions.explain: Step migration involves moving up a settlement hierarchy in stages, such as village to town to large city, rather than in one leap.

questions.q: Internal migration is best defined as movement that:
options: Only involves refugees
Occurs within the boundaries of a single country
Crosses an international border
Is always forced by conflict
questions.explain: Internal migration is movement within a country, such as rural-to-urban migration, rather than across national borders.

questions.q: A pro-natalist population policy is one that:
options: Encourages couples to have more children
Discourages childbearing
Forces emigration
Reduces life expectancy
questions.explain: Pro-natalist policies, used in some ageing-population countries, offer incentives to encourage higher birth rates.

questions.q: A challenge associated with an ageing population is:
options: An oversupply of school places for infants
A shrinking dependency ratio
Rising pension and healthcare costs with a smaller working-age tax base
A rapidly falling median age
questions.explain: Ageing populations increase the elderly dependency burden, raising pension and healthcare costs relative to the working population.

questions.q: A neo-Malthusian view of the population-resource relationship holds that:
options: Resource limits will ultimately constrain population growth
Resources are effectively infinite
Population can grow without any consequence
Innovation always outpaces population
questions.explain: Neo-Malthusians argue that finite resources and environmental limits will eventually check unsustainable population growth.

questions.q: The Epidemiological Transition describes the shift from:
options: Degenerative diseases back to infectious ones
Infectious and parasitic diseases to degenerative and lifestyle diseases as the main causes of death
No disease to all disease
Migration to non-migration
questions.explain: The epidemiological transition tracks the change in dominant causes of death from infectious diseases to chronic degenerative ones as countries develop.

questions.q: A demographic impact of immigration on a host country with an ageing population can be:
options: A rise in the average age to over 80
A fall in total population
An immediate end to all births
An increase in the working-age population, partly offsetting ageing
questions.explain: Immigrants are often of working age, which can rejuvenate the age structure and ease ageing-population pressures in the host country.

questions.q: The most rapid population growth in the Demographic Transition Model occurs in:
options: Stage 2, the early expanding phase, as death rates fall while birth rates stay high
Stage 4
Stage 1
Stage 5
questions.explain: In Stage 2 death rates fall sharply while birth rates remain high, producing rapid natural increase.

questions.q: A major contemporary international migration corridor is:
options: Deep ocean to mountain summit
Antarctica to the Arctic
The Moon to Mars
Mexico to the United States
questions.explain: The Mexico-to-USA corridor is one of the world's largest international migration flows, driven largely by economic factors.

questions.q: A refugee differs from an economic migrant primarily because a refugee:
options: Is forced to flee due to persecution, conflict or disaster
Never crosses a border
Always returns home within a year
Moves voluntarily for higher wages
questions.explain: A refugee is forced to leave to escape persecution, war or disaster, whereas an economic migrant moves chiefly for work.
